analysis.one_liner: Bars debt collectors from pursuing debts whose legal time limit to sue has expired.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without action in the House Financial Services Committee since April 2025 and has zero cosponsors, so no vote has ever been held.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to make it illegal for debt collectors to collect, or even try to collect, a debt whose statute of limitations has expired — the legal deadline for a creditor to sue [S2]. Today, collectors can still pursue these "time-barred" debts through calls and lawsuits; in many states, making a small payment or acknowledging the debt can restart the clock, which is why collectors often push people to do exactly that. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no further action [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers carrying old debt — especially people who lose a lawsuit over a time-barred debt or get talked into a payment that revives it — would gain a federal right not to be pursued at all once the legal deadline to sue has passed [S2]. It would also shift leverage away from debt buyers, who purchase very old debts for pennies and then press consumers for amounts courts could no longer enforce.

how_it_helps.text: It would create a flat federal prohibition: a debt collector may not collect or attempt to collect any consumer debt whose governing statute of limitations has expired, rather than leaving consumers to rely on a patchwork of state rules and court decisions [S2].

It closes a known trap: collectors can currently sue on time-barred debt, and a consumer who pays a little or acknowledges the debt can restart the limitations clock, resurrecting a debt that was no longer enforceable — which is why collectors have an incentive to solicit those payments.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collectors and debt buyers would lose the ability to pursue expired debts or use them as leverage for payments that revive the obligation. Original creditors — card issuers, medical providers, lenders — would recover less on aged accounts, which could nudge their pricing or write-off costs upward. Consumers who genuinely want to settle an old debt with a collector would lose the collector-initiated path to do so.

drawbacks.text: The ban is absolute: a time-barred debt may still be a debt the consumer honestly owes, and the bill prohibits collectors even from 'attempting to collect,' which could block collector-initiated settlement or payment-plan offers that some consumers might want [S2].

The bill does not address the underlying information problem — consumers often cannot tell whether a debt is time-barred, and the bill provides no new disclosure or documentation requirements, so collectors would still control most of the information in the exchange [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real and cheap for the public: it costs taxpayers nothing and simply removes a collection tactic that turns legally expired debts into fresh lawsuits and revived obligations. The main honest cost falls on collectors and creditors, who lose recovery on aged accounts, and on consumers who might have preferred to settle an old debt voluntarily — though the blanket "attempt to collect" ban is broader than a more tailored approach would be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and has seen no hearing, vote, or cosponsor since, so it is effectively dormant while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on April 8, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee that handles debt collection law [S4].
No cosponsors have joined, and the action history shows nothing after the referral — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collectors and debt buyers are better off for now: with the bill dormant, they can continue pursuing time-barred debts and soliciting payments that revive them, and creditors keep recourse on aged accounts.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only momentum; no other member has joined him

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair French Hill)
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill without any hearing, markup, or vote since April 2025

sides.party_line_note: No vote or recorded opposition exists; what is known is that a lone Democrat introduced the bill, zero members of either party signed on, and a Republican-run committee has not acted on it [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The industry's business model depends in part on buying old debts cheaply and pressing consumers to pay or settle them; the bill would flatly bar collection or attempted collection once the statute of limitations runs out [S2]. The industry's interest in recovering expired debts runs directly against the consumer protection the bill provides.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and other original creditors
industries.note: Creditors would lose a route to recover aged, charged-off accounts, either directly or through sales to debt buyers, which could modestly raise costs passed to other borrowers. Their interest in this bill is indirect and mostly channeled through the collection industry.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action in months, and a House committee controlled by the opposing party, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or a vote this Congress and will probably die quietly at its end unless reintroduced.
